reader_conclusion: The actual-versus-counterfactual hindcasts support bounded attribution of 2020-season extreme hurricane rainfall; they do not directly establish all hurricane hazards, trajectories, or future-season effects.

claims.content: For observed 2020 storms of at least tropical-storm strength, the hindcast attribution estimated that human-induced warming increased the 99th-percentile 3-hour rainfall rate by 10.2% (95% CI 5.1–15.5%) and 3-day accumulated rainfall by 4.8% (95% CI 0.1–9.5%).

evidence_relations.reason: The actual-versus-counterfactual ensemble comparison directly reports the two extreme-rainfall attribution estimates and bootstrap intervals.

support.source_location: Results: Attribution of hurricane season extreme rainfall; Fig. 4
support.reason: The claim preserves the model, season, storm-strength threshold, percentile endpoint, and uncertainty intervals.

claims.content: For observed storms at hurricane strength, the corresponding estimated anthropogenic increases were 11.3% for extreme 3-hour rainfall rates and 7.8% for extreme 3-day rainfall accumulations.

evidence_relations.reason: The hurricane-strength subset analysis directly reports the 11.3% and 7.8% attribution estimates with confidence intervals.

support.reason: The bounded hurricane-strength estimates are directly reported within the same hindcast framework.

claims.content: The study establishes that human-induced climate change increased hurricane hazards generally in 2020 and predicts similar effects across future hurricane seasons.

evidence_relations.reason: The evidence supports extreme rainfall endpoints, not wind, surge, genesis, or all hurricane hazards.
The hurricane subset strengthens the rainfall result but remains a single-season hindcast attribution.

support.reason: The source is strong for 2020 extreme rainfall under its hindcast design, but not for every hurricane hazard or future-season magnitude; dynamical fields were intentionally not adjusted in the counterfactual simulations.

author_boundary.summary: The authors explicitly bound the attribution to 2020 hurricane-season rainfall and state that the counterfactual simulations do not adjust storm dynamics, leaving other hazards and future-season effects outside the demonstrated result.
author_boundary.source_location: Discussion; limitations of the counterfactual setup and 2020-season rainfall scope

reasoning_edges.added_reach: Uses actual-versus-counterfactual hindcast ensembles to attribute a bounded extreme-rainfall difference to anthropogenic warming.
assumptions: The counterfactual SST/thermodynamic adjustments and fixed dynamical setup provide an adequate attribution contrast for these rainfall endpoints.

reasoning_edges.added_reach: Attributes the bounded hurricane-strength extreme-rainfall differences to anthropogenic warming in the model contrast.
assumptions: The hurricane-strength subset and hindcast ensembles preserve the intended counterfactual comparison.

reasoning_edges.added_reach: Extends a single-season extreme-rainfall attribution to all hurricane hazards and future seasons.
assumptions: The thermodynamic rainfall signal transfers unchanged to other hazards and future seasonal storm dynamics.

usable.results: The 2020 actual/counterfactual extreme-rainfall estimates and bootstrap intervals are directly usable.
usable.methods_or_design: The season-wide hindcast framework is useful for bounded attribution beyond single named storms.
usable.materials_or_documentation: Model configuration, initialization schedule, counterfactual construction, storm tracking, data, and code availability are documented.

downweight.worth_noticing: The study moves attribution from selected individual storms to a full observed hurricane season.
downweight.cautious_or_ignore: Do not broaden extreme-rainfall attribution into all hurricane hazards or unqualified future-season prediction.

uncertainty_and_follow_up: Future seasons, alternative models, and hazard-specific counterfactuals would test generality beyond 2020 extreme rainfall.
